questions.question: What is the time complexity of common array operations in Java?
questions.title: Array Operations Time Complexity | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Array access by index is O(1)** because memory is contiguous and offset-calculated. **Insertion or deletion in the middle is O(n)** because elements must shift. **Search is O(n)** for unsorted arrays.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the memory model behind arrays and can reason about why complexities are what they are
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying insertion is O(1) — only appending to the end is O(1); inserting in the middle requires shifting
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that O(1) access comes from the contiguous memory layout and direct address calculation

sections.title: Why Arrays Have O(1) Access
sections.content: Arrays store elements in **contiguous memory**. To access index `i`, Java computes `baseAddress + i * elementSize` — a single arithmetic operation regardless of array size, hence **O(1)**. However, inserting at the middle requires shifting all elements to the right by one position — that's **O(n)** in the worst case. Appending to the end (if space exists) is O(1).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Access by index: O(1)
- Search (unsorted): O(n) — must scan every element
- Search (sorted): O(log n) with binary search
- Insert at end: O(1) amortized (for ArrayList)
- Insert at middle/beginning: O(n) — elements shift
- Delete at middle: O(n) — elements shift
- Fixed size in Java — arrays cannot grow (use ArrayList for dynamic)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Arrays in Java store elements in contiguous memory, which is why index access is O(1) — it's just a memory address calculation. But inserting in the middle is O(n) because you have to shift every element after the insertion point one position to the right. Searching an unsorted array is O(n) because you may need to look at every element. If the array is sorted, you can use binary search for O(log n). I always distinguish between access, search, insert, and delete because they have very different complexities.

beats.text: An array is a fixed-size block of contiguous memory. Java computes any element's address as baseAddress plus index times element size — one math step, no searching. That's why access is always O(1) regardless of how big the array is.

Contiguous memory lets the CPU jump directly to any slot. It's the simplest and fastest data structure for random reads. We pay the price when we need to insert or delete — everything after the gap must shift.

Search unsorted: O(n) — scan every element
Search sorted: O(log n) — binary search halves the range
Insert at end: O(1) amortized for ArrayList
Insert at middle: O(n) — elements shift right
Delete at middle: O(n) — elements shift left

questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Java without using built-in reverse methods?
questions.title: Reverse String in Java | Fresher Interview Question
questions.direct_answer: **Convert to char array and swap from both ends toward the center.** Use two pointers — one at the start and one at the end — swapping characters until they meet. This is O(n) time and O(n) space (for the char array).

interviewer_intent.testing: Two-pointer technique, understanding of String immutability in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to modify a String directly — Java Strings are immutable; you must use a char array or StringBuilder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that StringBuilder.reverse() exists but show you know how to do it manually, and note String immutability

sections.title: String Immutability and the Two-Pointer Approach
sections.content: Java **Strings are immutable** — you cannot change characters in place. To reverse, convert to `char[]` with `toCharArray()`, then apply the two-pointer swap: pointer `left` starts at 0, pointer `right` starts at `length-1`. Swap `chars[left]` and `chars[right]`, then move `left++` and `right--` until they meet. Finally, `new String(chars)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Strings are immutable in Java — cannot modify in place
- `toCharArray()` gives you a mutable char array
- Two-pointer swap: left=0, right=n-1, swap, move inward
- Time: O(n), Space: O(n) for char array
- StringBuilder.reverse() is the production shortcut
- For palindrome check, use same two-pointer without fully reversing

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: First I'd mention that Java Strings are immutable, so I can't modify them in place. I'd convert to a char array, then use two pointers — one starting at the beginning, one at the end — swapping characters and moving inward until they meet. That's O(n) time and O(n) space for the char array. I'd also mention that StringBuilder has a built-in reverse method which is what you'd use in production, but the two-pointer approach shows the underlying algorithm.

beats.text: Reversing a string in Java requires acknowledging that Strings are immutable — you can't change a character at position i in place. The fix is converting to a char[], which is mutable, performing the swap there, then wrapping it back into a new String.
String immutability exists for thread safety and string pool optimisation. It's a deliberate Java design choice, not a bug. Once you know this, the char array workaround becomes the obvious pattern.

items: Step 1: call toCharArray() to get a mutable copy
Step 2: place left pointer at 0, right pointer at length minus 1
Step 3: swap chars[left] and chars[right], advance both pointers inward
Step 4: loop until left is no longer less than right
Step 5: return new String(chars)

Result: 'olleh'. non-obvious: the while loop condition 'left less than right' naturally handles both odd and even length strings without extra checks.

items: Trying to do str.charAt(i) = x will not compile — Strings don't have setters.
Forgetting to use a temp variable for the swap will overwrite one character before saving it.

questions.question: How do you find duplicates in an array in Java?
questions.title: Find Duplicates in Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use a HashSet for O(n) time.** Iterate the array — if the element is already in the set, it's a duplicate; otherwise add it. The brute-force nested loop approach is O(n²) and should be avoided.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you naturally reach for a HashSet for O(1) lookup instead of nested loops
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a nested loop O(n²) solution without mentioning the HashSet optimization
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Start with the brute force, state its complexity, then optimize to HashSet — showing your thought process

sections.title: HashSet for O(n) Duplicate Detection
sections.content: **Brute force**: for each element, scan all remaining elements — O(n²). **Optimized**: use a `HashSet<Integer>`. Iterate once — `contains()` is O(1) average. If the element is already in the set, it's a duplicate. If not, add it. Total: **O(n) time, O(n) space**. If space is a constraint and array contains integers 1 to n, you can use index-marking (negative marking) for O(1) space.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HashSet approach: O(n) time, O(n) space
- Nested loop approach: O(n²) time, O(1) space
- HashSet.contains() is O(1) average (O(n) worst case)
- Sorting approach: sort first O(n log n), then scan adjacent pairs O(n)
- For integers 1-n: index-flipping trick for O(n) time O(1) space
- Always discuss the tradeoff when giving your solution

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: My first instinct is the HashSet approach. I iterate through the array once, and for each element I check if it's already in the set — if yes, it's a duplicate; if no, I add it. That's O(n) time because HashSet lookups are O(1) average, but O(n) space. If the interviewer asks for O(1) space and the array contains integers from 1 to n, I'd use the index-flipping trick where I negate the value at the index corresponding to each element. I always mention the brute force first so the interviewer can see the progression.

questions.question: What is the two-sum problem and how do you solve it efficiently?
questions.title: Two Sum Problem Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two-sum**: given an array and a target, find two indices whose values sum to the target. The optimal solution uses a **HashMap for O(n) time** — store each element as key with its index as value, then for each element check if `target - element` is already in the map.

interviewer_intent.testing: HashMap-based optimization, recognizing the complement pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only giving the O(n²) brute force or using a sorted-array approach that returns values not indices
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you store the complement's index in the map so you return indices, not just confirm a pair exists

sections.title: The Complement Pattern with HashMap
sections.content: For each element `nums[i]`, the **complement** is `target - nums[i]`. If the complement has already been seen, we found our pair. Use a `HashMap<Integer, Integer>` mapping value→index. Iterate once: check if complement is in map — if yes, return `[map.get(complement), i]`; if no, put `nums[i]→i` in the map. **O(n) time, O(n) space.**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Brute force: two nested loops → O(n²)
- HashMap approach: O(n) time, O(n) space
- Key insight: for each element, ask 'have I seen target minus this element?'
- Store value→index in map to return indices
- Sorted two-pointer: O(n log n) sort + O(n) scan — works if you need values not indices
- This problem appears in almost every fresher interview

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd start by noting that the brute force — checking every pair — is O(n squared). The optimal approach uses a HashMap. I iterate through the array once; for each element I compute its complement, which is target minus the current value, and check if that complement is already in the map. If it is, I return the current index and the stored index. If it's not, I add the current value and its index to the map. This is O(n) time and O(n) space. I make sure to clarify whether the problem wants indices or values before starting.

questions.question: How do you check if two strings are anagrams of each other?
questions.title: Check Anagram Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same frequencies.** Use a frequency array (int[26] for lowercase) or a HashMap. Sort-and-compare is simpler but O(n log n); frequency count is O(n).

interviewer_intent.testing: Frequency counting pattern, knowing multiple approaches and their tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing the sorting approach without the O(n) frequency count alternative
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Offer both approaches and explain when you'd use each — sorting is simpler, frequency count is faster

sections.title: Two Approaches: Sort vs Frequency Count
sections.content: **Approach 1 (Sort)**: Sort both strings and compare — `Arrays.sort(s1.toCharArray())` — O(n log n). Simple but slower. **Approach 2 (Frequency Array)**: Create `int[26]`, increment for chars in s1, decrement for chars in s2. If all entries are 0, they're anagrams — **O(n) time, O(1) space** (the array is fixed size 26). First check lengths — if they differ, immediately return false.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Early exit: if lengths differ, return false immediately
- Sort approach: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for char arrays
- Frequency array: O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed 26 chars)
- HashMap approach: O(n) time, O(k) space where k = unique chars (handles Unicode)
- `char - 'a'` converts a character to array index 0-25
- This pattern extends to 'group anagrams' and 'find all anagrams in string'

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: My preferred approach is the frequency array. First I check if the lengths are equal — if not, they can't be anagrams and I return false immediately. Then I create an integer array of size 26, iterate through the first string incrementing counts, and iterate through the second string decrementing counts. If all 26 entries are zero at the end, they're anagrams. This is O(n) time and O(1) space since the array is a fixed size. I'd also mention the simpler sort-and-compare approach as an alternative, noting it's O(n log n).

followup_questions: How would you group a list of strings by anagram?
How do you find all anagram substrings in a string?

questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique and when do you use it on arrays?
questions.title: Two Pointer Technique Arrays
questions.direct_answer: The two-pointer technique uses two indices that move toward each other or in the same direction to solve array problems in O(n) instead of O(n²).

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to optimize brute-force solutions using a classic pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops when two pointers would reduce complexity
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific problems it solves and mention the sorted-array prerequisite

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two-pointer technique is a pattern where you maintain two indices into an array and move them based on some condition, rather than using nested loops. The most common variant starts one pointer at the beginning and one at the end and moves them toward each other.

The classic use case is checking whether an array has a pair that sums to a target. With a sorted array, you place left at index 0 and right at the last index. If the sum equals the target you return true; if it's too small you move left forward; if it's too large you move right backward. This is O(n) instead of the brute-force O(n²).

Another common variant is the fast-slow pointer, where both pointers start at the same end but move at different speeds. This is used for detecting cycles in linked lists and for problems like removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place.

The key prerequisite for the converging variant is that the array must be sorted, or you must understand why your problem's invariant holds as the pointers move. For strings, the same idea applies to palindrome checking — compare characters at both ends and move inward.

In interviews I always ask myself: can I replace a nested loop with two pointers? If the inner loop is just scanning for a complement or a boundary, two pointers usually work and halves the time complexity.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Converging pointers: left at 0, right at end — move based on comparison (requires sorted input)
Same-direction pointers: fast/slow — used for duplicates removal, cycle detection
Reduces O(n²) nested loop to O(n) single pass
Common problems: two-sum on sorted array, palindrome check, container with most water

No inner loop needed. One pass of the array handles work that a nested loop would take n squared steps to do.

Nested loops are the intuitive but slow solution for pair-finding problems. Two pointers work when the data has a sorted or structured property that lets you decide which pointer to move, eliminating the need to check every combination.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm)?
questions.title: Kadane's Algorithm Maximum Subarray
questions.direct_answer: Kadane's algorithm scans the array once, keeping a running sum and a global maximum, achieving O(n) time and O(1) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of dynamic programming thinking at a basic level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Resetting the running sum to zero instead of to the current element when it goes negative
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the intuition: 'If carrying the previous sum hurts me, I start fresh from here'

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kadane's algorithm solves the maximum subarray problem in a single pass. The intuition is: at every position, you decide whether it's better to extend the existing subarray or start a new one from the current element.

You maintain two variables: currentSum and maxSum. For each element, you set currentSum to the maximum of the element itself versus currentSum plus the element. This is saying: if my running sum has gone so negative that adding this element alone would be better, then start fresh here. Then you update maxSum if currentSum is larger.

The code looks like this in Java: initialize currentSum and maxSum to the first element, then loop from index 1. At each step: currentSum = Math.max(arr[i], currentSum + arr[i]); maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, currentSum).

Initializing to the first element rather than zero is important because it handles all-negative arrays correctly — if every number is negative, the answer is the least negative number, not zero.

This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space since we only store two integers regardless of input size. A brute-force approach would check all subarrays in O(n²) or O(n³).

Interviewers often follow up by asking you to also return the start and end indices of the subarray, which requires tracking when you restart and when you update the maximum.

sections.title: Key Points
content: currentSum = Math.max(arr[i], currentSum + arr[i]) — extend or restart
Initialize both variables to arr[0], not 0, to handle all-negative arrays
O(n) time, O(1) space — single pass, two variables
To track indices: record start when restarting, record end when maxSum updates

followup_questions: How do you return the actual subarray, not just the sum?
Does Kadane's work if all numbers are negative?

speakable_v2.hook: Kadane's algorithm is one decision repeated n times — extend or restart — and that single idea beats O(n²) brute force.

beats.text: Kadane's algorithm finds the contiguous subarray with the largest sum in a single pass. It keeps two values: currentSum (the best sum ending at the current position) and maxSum (the best seen globally). At each element it asks: 'Am I better off extending what I have, or starting fresh here?'

Brute force checks every possible subarray — O(n²) or worse. Kadane's is O(n) because the extend-or-restart decision means we never need to go back. It's essentially the simplest form of dynamic programming.

items: Initialise: currentSum = arr[0], maxSum = arr[0]
For each element from index 1: currentSum = Math.max(arr[i], currentSum + arr[i])
Update: maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, currentSum)
Return maxSum after the loop

beats.text: Array [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]. Walking through: currentSum becomes 1 at index 1, drops to -2 but resets to 4 at index 3, climbs to 6 at index 7, ending with maxSum of 6 for the subarray [4, -1, 2, 1]. candidates miss: initialise to arr[0] not 0 — if all numbers are negative, the answer is the least negative element, not zero, and zero initialisation gives the wrong result.

items: Initialising currentSum and maxSum to 0 breaks all-negative arrays — always use arr[0].
Resetting currentSum to 0 instead of arr[i] when restarting is a common coding slip.

questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Java without using library methods?
questions.title: Reverse String Java Without Library
questions.direct_answer: Convert to a char array, swap characters from both ends moving inward using two pointers, then build a new String from the modified array.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Strings are immutable in Java and basic array manipulation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to modify a String directly instead of converting to char array first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention immutability as the reason you need the char array, and compare to StringBuilder.reverse()

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The key thing to remember about reversing a string in Java is that Strings are immutable — you cannot change characters in place. So the first step is converting the String to a char array using toCharArray().

Once you have the char array, you apply the two-pointer swap pattern. Place left at index 0 and right at the last index. While left is less than right, swap the characters at those positions and move both pointers inward. After the loop, construct a new String from the modified array using new String(chars).

The full approach: char[] chars = str.toCharArray(); then a while loop with the swap using a temporary variable, then return new String(chars). This is O(n) time and O(n) space because of the char array.

In a real project I'd use StringBuilder's reverse() method, which is cleaner and handles edge cases. But for an interview without library methods, the char array plus two-pointer swap is the expected answer.

Edge cases worth mentioning: an empty string or single-character string should return as-is — the while loop naturally handles these since left would not be less than right. Also, this approach works correctly for even and odd length strings since you're swapping until the pointers meet or cross.

content: Strings are immutable — convert to char[] first with toCharArray()
Two-pointer swap: while(left < right) swap chars[left++] and chars[right--]
Return new String(chars) to build the result

speakable_v2.hook: Reversing a string without libraries is a two-line idea wrapped in a Java gotcha — strings aren't modifiable.

beats.text: To reverse a string without library methods you need a mutable character sequence. Java's String is immutable so you can't change it in place. The workaround is toCharArray() which gives you a char[] you can modify. Then do a two-pointer swap and wrap it back into a String.

String immutability is a deliberate design for thread safety and intern pool optimisation. It means every string operation returns a new object — which is why char[] is the escape hatch when you need in-place work.

items: Step 1: char[] chars = str.toCharArray()
Step 2: int left = 0, right = chars.length - 1
Step 3: while left less than right — swap chars[left] and chars[right], then move both pointers
Step 4: return new String(chars)

beats.text: Input 'Java': chars = [J, a, v, a]. Swap J and a → [a, a, v, J]. Swap a and v → [a, v, a, J]. Pointers cross, done. Result: 'avaJ'. non-obvious: an empty string or single character goes through the while loop zero times and comes out unchanged — no special case needed.

items: You can't do str.charAt(i) = x — String has no setter, that won't compile.
Forgetting the temp variable in the swap overwrites one character before saving it.
